questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The First Printed Books' refers to.
questions.a: The earliest kind of print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea, where books were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks; from hand-printing, the technology moved to mechanical printing, with the imperial state in China being the major producer of printed material for nearly five centuries.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The First Printed Books'.
questions.a: Print technology originated in East Asia through woodblock printing on paper, with China producing the earliest printed books long before mechanical printing reached Europe.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The First Printed Books' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The First Printed Books

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Print in Japan' refers to.
questions.a: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around AD 768-770; the oldest Japanese book, the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, was printed in AD 868, and by the seventeenth century urban printing in Edo (Tokyo) produced illustrated books for a growing literate public.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Print in Japan'.
questions.a: Japan adopted woodblock printing through Buddhist missionaries from China and developed a flourishing illustrated print culture by the seventeenth century.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Print in Japan' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Print in Japan

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Print Comes to Europe' refers to.
questions.a: Print technology reached Europe through trade and the silk route; by the fifteenth century woodblock printing was common in Europe for printing textiles and playing cards, and merchants and students began demanding cheaper books, leading to the development of a printing system with movable type.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Print Comes to Europe'.
questions.a: The demand for cheaper books from students, merchants and the growing literate public in fifteenth-century Europe drove the shift from woodblock printing to movable type printing.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Print Comes to Europe' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Print Comes to Europe

questions.a: 8 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Gutenberg and the Printing Press' refers to.
questions.a: Johann Gutenberg developed the first known printing press in the 1440s, adapting olive press technology and creating movable metal type; the first book he printed was the Bible in 1448, marking the shift from hand-copying to mechanical printing in Europe.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gutenberg and the Printing Press'.
questions.a: Gutenberg's printing press, built by adapting the olive press and movable metal type, made the mass production of identical books possible and began the print revolution in Europe.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Gutenberg and the Printing Press' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Gutenberg and the Printing Press

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Print Revolution' refers to.
questions.a: The print revolution, set off by Gutenberg's press, transformed the production of books from hand-copying by scribes to mechanical printing, drastically reducing the cost and time of producing books and making them accessible to a far wider public across Europe.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Print Revolution'.
questions.a: The print revolution shifted book production from slow hand-copying to fast mechanical printing, making books cheaper and widely available and transforming social and intellectual life.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Print Revolution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Print Revolution and Its Impact

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Reading Mania' refers to.
questions.a: Through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the literacy rate went up in most parts of Europe, and churches of different denominations set up schools in villages, producing a reading mania among the common people who eagerly read books, pamphlets, almanacs and chapbooks.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Reading Mania'.
questions.a: Rising literacy and village schools created a 'reading mania' in seventeenth and eighteenth century Europe, as common people sought cheap printed material for entertainment, information and devotion.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Reading Mania' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Reading Mania

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Nineteenth Century' refers to.
questions.a: In the nineteenth century the print industry expanded with hand presses giving way to power-driven cylindrical presses, cheap serialised novels and penny magazines reaching new working-class readers, and women and children becoming important new readers and writers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Nineteenth Century'.
questions.a: The nineteenth century saw mass production of cheap print through power-driven presses, creating new readers among the working class, women and children, and turning publishing into a major industry.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Nineteenth Century' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Nineteenth Century

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India and the World of Print' refers to.
questions.a: India had a rich tradition of hand-written manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian, but they were expensive and fragile; the first printing press was brought to Goa by Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century, and by the late eighteenth century newspapers and books began to be printed in Indian languages.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India and the World of Print'.
questions.a: Print entered India through Portuguese missionaries in Goa, and over time replaced costly hand-written manuscripts with cheaper printed books in Indian languages.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India and the World of Print' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India and the World of Print

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Religious Reform and Public Debates' refers to.
questions.a: From the early nineteenth century, print enabled religious reformers and orthodox sections to debate ideas through tracts and newspapers; Raja Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi to campaign against sati, while orthodox Hindus published the Samachar Chandrika to defend tradition, making print a vehicle for public debate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Religious Reform and Public Debates'.
questions.a: Print created a new public sphere in nineteenth-century India where reformers and orthodox groups used newspapers and tracts to debate religious and social issues such as sati and widow remarriage.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Religious Reform and Public Debates' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Religious Reform and Public Debates

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Censorship in Nineteenth-Century India' refers to.
questions.a: The colonial government introduced censorship to control printed material critical of British rule; after the revolt of 1857 the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was passed to silence criticism in Indian-language newspapers, while English-language papers remained free, showing the selective use of censorship.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Censorship in Nineteenth-Century India'.
questions.a: The colonial state used censorship laws like the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 to suppress criticism in Indian-language newspapers while allowing English-language papers greater freedom.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Censorship in Nineteenth-Century India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Censorship and the Colonial State
